chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: Ethel Waters records found at the House and the House's origin
summary: Records found there; the House was a little building bought in memory of Cliff Jackson, with a dorm and visiting musicians such as Vic Dickenson.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: a lot of Ethel Waters recordings here. I think the very first recording she ever made was here because I bought the house furnished. I have one of the first records she made of "Am I Blue". It's a blue record. And some of her earlier, Dianh Swan records.
No, "Am I Blue" was just a single tune.
Oh, "I Must Have That Man", that's the one I'm thinking of, sorry.
"Am I Blue" was a single that she made. I found quite a few things here that she made. So I'm here and I'm staying.
And The House That Jazz Built, that was Cliff Jackson?

Yeah, well the House That Jazz Built was a little building that we bought in 1956. And when we first had it, well first of all, Orville, my son was going to music school and I set it up so he would have a little studio over there. And there was a space over there for some of the musicians that were in and out of town. That was a place for them to leave their

trunk, and they had sort of a little dorm over there. Vic And/Dickenson lived there. Marcus Foster, Ron Scott, Jimmy Rainey, and in fact the Meade "Lux" Lewis stayed there on one of his engagements in New York. He stayed at the house and the night that he got killed he had just left from The House That Jazz Built. So after the guys, most of them got settled with apartments of their own - and then of course, there was nobody living there. This was Cliff's baby, you know. He went over and saw the boys every day and sort of kept the house up. But when the guys left we didn't have anybody staying there so a local anti-poverty program moved in there. And they were in there for three or four years. In the meantime Cliff passed in 1970 and I found myself in charge. By this time the house was in sort of a dilapidated state of affairs and I had to get those people out so I got together with Wilma Dobie, Dobey's, a friend of mine, and I had this idea in the back of my head for a long time. Anyway, I didn't have any idea of what we were going to call it so I came up with this thing, The House That Jazz Built. So in 1970, that's when we started thinking about it and we got the people out. In 1975 we had a dedication
